2003A16.goal: We want the units digit of $13^{2003}$. Only the units digit $3$ matters, and powers of $3$ cycle.
2003A16.approach: $2003\equiv3\pmod4$, so the units digit is the third in the cycle: $7$.

check.q: What is the units digit of $3^3$?

2003A16.shortcut: Every units-digit cycle divides $4$; reduce exponents mod $4$.
2003A16.recognize: Units digits of powers: cycle of length dividing $4$.

2003A17.goal: An equilateral triangle's perimeter equals the area of its circumcircle. We want the radius $R$. Relate the side to $R$.

check.q: For an equilateral triangle with circumradius $R$, what is the side?

2003A17.bridge: Write the perimeter in terms of $R$.
2003A17.shortcut: The units mismatch is deliberate: just set the numbers equal.

2003A18.goal: Sum of reciprocals of the roots of $\tfrac{2003}{2004}x+1+\tfrac1x=0$. Clear the fraction and use Vieta.
2003A18.recognize: Sums of reciprocal roots: $-\tfrac bc$, or substitute $y=1/x$.

2003A19.goal: A semicircle of diameter $1$ sits on a chord of length $1$ at the top of a semicircle of diameter $2$. We want the lune's area. Lune = small semicircle − the big circle's segment cut by that chord.

tools.name: Chord of length 1 in radius 1
tools.why: The chord and radii make an equilateral triangle.

tools.name: Segment
tools.why: $60^\circ$ sector of radius $1$ minus an equilateral triangle of side $1$.

check.q: What is the area of an equilateral triangle with side $1$?

2003A19.bridge: Small semicircle minus the big circle's segment.
solution: Big circle's segment over the chord: $\tfrac\pi6-\tfrac{\sqrt3}4$.
2003A19.shortcut: The lune is positive and small ($\approx0.30$).
traps: Subtracting the whole sector instead of the segment.
2003A19.recognize: Lunes: one circular region minus a segment of another.

2003A20.goal: A random three-digit number $n$ ($100$–$999$). We want $P(n\text{ is three digits in both base }9\text{ and base }11)$.
2003A20.approach: Base $9$: $81\le n\le728$. Base $11$: $121\le n\le1330$. Both with $100\le n\le999$: $121\le n\le728$: $608$ numbers. $\tfrac{608}{900}\approx0.68$.

check.q: What is the largest three-digit base-$9$ number in base $10$?

2003A21.goal: Choose $6$ cookies from $3$ kinds (plenty of each). Only the counts matter: solutions to $a+b+c=6$ in non-negative integers.

steps.title: Model
steps.explain: $6$ stars, $2$ bars: arrangements of $8$ symbols choosing bar positions.

check.why: One fewer than the number of kinds.

2003A21.shortcut: "At least six of each" just means no upper limits matter.
2003A21.recognize: Choosing a multiset of size $n$ from $k$ types: $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$.

2003A22.goal: Rectangle $AB=8$, $BC=9$; $BH=6$, $DE=4$; lines $EC$ and $AH$ meet at $G$, and $F$ is the foot from $G$ to line $AD$. We want $GF$. Use coordinates.
2003A22.bridge: Coordinates, intersect, read off the distance.
2003A22.shortcut: Similar triangles: the gap between the lines grows by $\tfrac14$ per unit of $x$, starting at $5$.
traps: Confusing which side $E$ is measured from.
2003A22.recognize: Lines extended outside a rectangle: coordinates make the intersection easy.

2003A23.goal: A triangle of toothpicks with $2003$ small triangles in its base row. We want the number of toothpicks. Every toothpick is a side of exactly one upward-pointing small triangle.

check.q: With $5$ small triangles in the base, how many upward ones are in that row?

2003A23.bridge: Each toothpick belongs to exactly one upward triangle.
2003A23.shortcut: Check with the example: $3$ rows, $6$ upward, $18$ toothpicks.

2003A24.goal: Red $1$–$5$ and blue $3$–$6$ alternate (R B R … R), each red dividing its blue neighbours. We want the sum of the middle three cards. Start with the most restricted cards.

tools.name: Restricted reds
tools.fact: R5\text{ only beside }B5;\ R4\text{ only beside }B4

tools.name: Ends
tools.fact: \text{a card with one possible neighbour sits at an end}
tools.why: Middle reds have two blue neighbours.

2003A24.approach: $R5$ and $R4$ are the two ends: $R5,B5,\ldots,B4,R4$. $B5$'s other neighbour divides $5$: $R1$. $R4$'s neighbour $B4$ needs another red dividing $4$: $R2$. Then $B6$ next to $R2$, and $R3$ between $B3$ and $B6$.

check.q: Which red cards can neighbour blue $5$?

steps.title: Middle
steps.explain: $R2$'s other neighbour is $B6$; the remaining $B3$ sits next to $R1$; $R3$ between $B3$ and $B6$. Stack $5,5,1,3,3,6,2,4,4$. Middle three: $3+3+6=12$.

check.q: Which blue card can be next to red $2$ besides $4$?

2003A24.bridge: Place the most constrained cards first.
2003A24.shortcut: Cards with only one legal neighbour must go at the ends.
2003A24.recognize: Arrangement puzzles: start with the most restricted pieces.

2003A25.shortcut: Quotient/remainder by $100$ mod $11$: like summing two-digit blocks.
2003A25.recognize: Splitting a number into blocks: blocks of $2$ digits sum to $n$ mod $99$ (hence mod $11$).
